selectionDetail: Justices are appointed from Alaska Judicial Council nominees, stand in a retention election at the first general election more than three years after appointment, then every ten years; the chief justice is chosen by peer vote for a three-year term (Susan Carney since 2025).
All nine justices, including the chief justice, are chosen in statewide partisan elections to six-year terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment until the next election.

All seven positions, including a separately elected chief justice, are chosen in statewide nonpartisan elections to eight-year terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment until the next election.

Justices are appointed from Commission on Appellate Court Appointments nominees, serve an initial term of at least two years, then stand in retention elections every six years; the chief justice is selected by peer vote (Ann Timmer since July 2024).

Justices are appointed by the governor with Commission on Judicial Appointments confirmation, then appear statewide in yes-no retention elections for 12-year terms; one seat vacant since Justice Jenkins retired October 31, 2025.

Justices are appointed from Supreme Court Nominating Commission nominees, serve a two-year provisional term, then stand in retention elections every ten years; the chief justice is chosen by peer vote (Monica Márquez since July 2024).

Justices are nominated by the governor from Judicial Selection Commission candidates and confirmed by the General Assembly to eight-year terms; no statewide ballot (chief justice Raheem Mullins since January 2025).

courtName: District of Columbia Court of Appeals
selectionDetail: Judges are appointed by the President from a D.C. Judicial Nomination Commission list with U.S. Senate confirmation to 15-year terms, never on any ballot; two of nine seats currently vacant.
Justices are nominated from Judicial Nominating Commission candidates and confirmed by the state Senate to 12-year terms, with a constitutional party-balance requirement; no statewide ballot.
Justices are appointed from a judicial nominating commission shortlist and thereafter appear statewide in yes-no retention elections for six-year terms.
Nine justices are chosen in statewide nonpartisan elections for six-year terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment, appointees then standing in the next nonpartisan election.

Justices are appointed from a Judicial Selection Commission shortlist with Senate confirmation for 10-year terms; reappointment is decided by the commission, never a ballot. One associate seat vacant after Devens's elevation to chief in May 2026.
Justices are appointed from a State Judicial Nominating Commission shortlist, stand in retention after one year, then every eight years.
Five justices are elected statewide in nonpartisan elections to six-year terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment from a judicial council list.

Seven justices are initially elected in partisan elections from five districts to 10-year terms, then face uncontested yes-no retention elections; midterm vacancies are filled by supreme court appointment until the next election.
Justices are appointed from a nominating-commission shortlist, stand in a statewide yes-no retention election after ~two years, then every 10 years.

Justices are appointed from a Supreme Court Nominating Commission shortlist and face statewide retention every six years; one seat vacant after Chief Justice Luckert's retirement Jan 2, 2026 (Rosen became chief by seniority).
Justices are elected in nonpartisan elections from seven appellate districts to eight-year terms; the chief justice is chosen by peer vote for four years.

Justices are elected in partisan elections from seven districts to ten-year terms; the most senior justice serves as chief, and midterm vacancies are filled by interim appointment pending a special election.
Justices are appointed by the governor with Governor's Council approval and serve until mandatory retirement at 70; never on a statewide ballot (term-end years are age-70 retirement dates).

Justices are appointed from a nominating-commission list with Senate confirmation, then stand in yes-no retention elections for ten-year terms; renamed from Maryland Court of Appeals in December 2022.
Justices are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Maine Senate to seven-year terms; no statewide ballot.
Justices are nominated by parties but elected statewide on a nonpartisan ballot to eight-year terms; the chief justice is elected by the justices (Megan Cavanagh since 2025).
Justices are elected statewide in nonpartisan elections to six-year terms (most first reach the court by appointment to an interim vacancy); the chief justice is a directly elected statewide seat.

Judges are appointed from a nominating commission's list under the Missouri Plan, then stand in yes-no retention elections for 12-year terms; the chief justice is elected by peer vote to a two-year term.

Nine justices are elected in nonpartisan elections, three per district, to eight-year terms; the chief is the most senior justice. Two District 3 seats are vacant (Chamberlin and Maxwell resigned Dec 2025 for federal judgeships; special elections Nov 2026).
Justices are chosen in statewide nonpartisan elections for eight-year terms; the chief justice is separately elected to that position; unopposed incumbents stand in retention-style yes-no votes.

Justices are chosen in statewide partisan elections for eight-year terms; the chief justice is elected by voters to that office, and midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment until the next general election.

Justices are chosen in statewide nonpartisan elections for ten-year terms; the governor fills midterm vacancies, and the chief justice is chosen by vote of the supreme and district court judges (Lisa Fair McEvers became chief in 2026).
Justices are appointed from a judicial nominating commission's list, then face yes-no retention elections every six years; the chief justice runs statewide, associates by district.
Justices are nominated by the governor and confirmed by the Executive Council, serving until mandatory retirement at 70 with no elections of any kind.
Justices are appointed by the governor with senate consent for an initial seven-year term, then may be reappointed to serve until mandatory retirement at 70; never on a ballot.

Hybrid: vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment from a commission list, the appointee runs in a statewide partisan election at the next general, and thereafter stands in retention elections (57% yes) for eight-year terms.
Justices are chosen in statewide nonpartisan elections for six-year terms (vacancies filled by gubernatorial appointment until the next election); the chief justice rotates by seniority.

NY's court of last resort (its 'Supreme Court' is the trial court); judges are appointed from a Commission on Judicial Nomination shortlist with senate confirmation to 14-year terms and never appear on a ballot.

Justices run statewide for six-year terms with party labels on the general-election ballot (2021 law); the chief justice is elected by voters to that office; gubernatorial appointees fill midterm vacancies until the next general election.
Judges are appointed from a nominating-commission list and appear on yes-no retention ballots every six years; Presiding Judge Gary Lumpkin retires effective 2027-01-01.

Justices are appointed from a nominating-commission list and appear on yes-no retention ballots — first at the next general election after a year in office, then every six years (Kauger lost retention Nov 2024; successor Travis Jett faces retention 2026).

Justices are chosen in statewide nonpartisan elections for six-year terms; the governor fills midterm vacancies with the appointee standing at the next general election; the chief justice is selected by peer vote.

Justices are first elected in statewide partisan elections, then keep seats via yes-no retention every ten years (Donohue, Dougherty, Wecht retained Nov 2025); the chief justice is the longest-serving justice.
Justices are appointed by the governor from a nominating-commission list, confirmed by both chambers, and serve for life — never on any ballot; one seat is vacant as of July 2026.
Justices are elected by the General Assembly to 10-year terms after Judicial Merit Selection Commission screening; there is no statewide ballot.
Justices are appointed by the governor from nominating-commission recommendations, stand in a yes-no retention election after at least three years, then every eight years.
Justices are appointed by the governor with legislative confirmation, then stand in yes-no retention elections for eight-year terms; the justices select the chief from among themselves.

Judges of Texas's court of last resort for criminal cases are elected statewide in partisan elections to six-year staggered terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment until the next general election.
Justices are elected statewide in partisan elections to six-year staggered terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment with Senate confirmation until the next general election.

Justices are appointed by the governor with Senate confirmation and stand in yes-no retention elections (first after at least three years, then every ten years); the court expanded from five to seven seats in 2026 and one seat remains vacant as of July 2026.
Justices are elected by majority vote of both houses of the General Assembly to 12-year terms and never appear on a voter's ballot; the chief justice is chosen by peer vote.
Justices are appointed by the governor from judicial nominating board candidates with Senate confirmation, retained for successive six-year terms by General Assembly vote; no statewide ballot.
Nine justices are elected statewide in nonpartisan elections to staggered six-year terms; midterm vacancies are filled by gubernatorial appointment, appointees standing at the next general election.

Seven justices are elected statewide in nonpartisan spring elections to 10-year terms (at most one seat per year); the chief justice is chosen by peer vote for two years. Rebecca Bradley's term expires July 31, 2026.

courtName: Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia
selectionDetail: Five justices are elected statewide in nonpartisan elections (partisan before 2016) to 12-year terms; the chief justice rotates by peer vote annually. Flanigan and Kirkpatrick were seated June 2026 after winning May 2026 elections for unexpired terms.
Justices are appointed from a judicial nominating commission's list, stand in retention at the first general election after one year, then every eight years; the chief justice is chosen by peer vote.
